items.title: Job openings posted big September gain in positive sign for labor market ahead of payrolls report
items.summary: The BLS reported job openings at 7.52 million, up 333,000 from August and well above the Dow Jones consensus outlook for 7.15 million
items.body: Job openings surged in September, as did the number of workers who quit their positions, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday, while hiring also rose and layoffs dropped. In its monthly look at labor market slack and worker mobility, the BLS reported job openings at 7.52 million, up 333,000 from August and well above the Dow Jones consensus outlook for 7.15 million. As a share of the total workforce, the rate of job openings increased to 4.5%, up 0.2 percentage point from the prior month, according to the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey . There are now some 414,000 more job openings than workers classified as unemployed, or about 1.05 openings to every available worker. Openings rose in manufacturing (54,000) as well as state and local government (108,000) and professional and business services (106,000).

items.title: Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade
items.summary: Lessons from the $6.3 billion Binance hack could help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade.
items.body: The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets. Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus. Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout , protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.

items.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
items.summary: The food deal, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month, is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far.
items.body: The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month. The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders. The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

items.title: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
items.summary: Firm reveals details about how its cryptocurrency exchange was compromised, saying operation began in June The hackers behind the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance heist used bogus job interviews, malicious software and an internal AI tool, the company has revealed. The world’s largest…
items.body: The hackers behind the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance heist used bogus job interviews, malicious software and an internal AI tool, the company has revealed. The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange was compromised in an operation that began with an inadvertent download of malware in June, led to a recruitment scam in September and then a raid last week of “hot wallets” where billions of dollars worth of crypto-assets were taken. The FBI has blamed North Korea for last week’s heist but Pyongyang, a prolific crypto-hacker , described the accusation as “absurd rhetoric” on Tuesday. According to an update Binance released on Tuesday, the hackers got their first foothold in the summer when a company engineer inadvertently downloaded malware that exposed the employee’s role and that of others in the team that looked after Binance’s cryptowallet infrastructure.

items.title: Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?
items.summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.
items.body: With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital. Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon , Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros. Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars. Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

items.title: China’s scrap dealers are scrambling for waste. So why is the recycling sector booming?
items.summary: Shanghai scrap collector Li Jie has a problem, one which would appear unusual to most: trash is getting too valuable. “Ordinary recyclables like cardboard and plastic are now hard to come by,” he said. “Their prices have risen so much that there are so many collectors, including…
items.body: Shanghai scrap collector Li Jie has a problem, one which would appear unusual to most: trash is getting too valuable. “Ordinary recyclables like cardboard and plastic are now hard to come by,” he said. “Their prices have risen so much that there are so many collectors, including many companies.” The wave of new players has made it harder to find those materials, and others such as copper and aluminium. But even at small volumes, he said, the business remains profitable and he has no desire to leave. In the first nine months of this year, revenue in mainland China’s waste recycling sector was up 1.8 per cent year on year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, but profits jumped 63 per cent.

items.title: AMD stock jumps 8% on earnings as data center revenue nearly doubles
items.summary: AMD reported better-than-expected third-quarter results, driven by booming sales of AI chips
items.body: Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jump 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock jumped 8% in extended trading. CEO Lisa Su said in a press release that she expects growth in data center processors to "accelerate further," and that meeting demand won't be a problem. "With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years " Su said in a statement. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But the stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand .

items.title: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia's decision was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year.
items.body: Australia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008. The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year. In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March. The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast.

items.title: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit
items.summary: The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman.
items.body: The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman. The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday. Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship. "The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box ." Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday.

items.title: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
items.summary: The regulator says it supports lenders offering early compensation offers, as long as they are fair.
items.body: Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga. Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme. That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year. But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit. The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case. Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner.

items.title: Protect Poundland from predatory capitalism, MPs tell government
items.summary: Budget retailer and 12,000 jobs at risk after US owner fails to accept buyout offers MPs have called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping. The fate of the retail chain and its 12,000 staff remains…
items.body: MPs have called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping. The fate of the retail chain and its 12,000 staff remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday. The board of Poundland has lined up the advisory company AlixPartners to run the process after the owner, US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, ceased providing funding. In an urgent question in the House of Commons on Tuesday, Gareth Snell, Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent Central , asked the government what could be done to “send a message to Gordon Brothers that the predatory capitalism that they are putting into this company will not be tolerated, because we in this country will always stand with people before profit”.

items.title: PBOC pledges support for stocks as China’s market slide defies rescue efforts
items.summary: China’s central bank governor has reaffirmed support for the country’s beleaguered stock market after a series of rescue measures failed to put a floor under plummeting share prices. Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), pledged in a work report presented…
items.body: China’s central bank governor has reaffirmed support for the country’s beleaguered stock market after a series of rescue measures failed to put a floor under plummeting share prices. Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), pledged in a work report presented to the standing committee of the National People’s Congress on Tuesday that more actions would be taken to ease financial risks in key areas, including the capital market and the property sector. “Monetary policy tools will be effectively implemented to buoy the capital market,” Pan said in the report, according to state news agency Xinhua.

items.title: Apple warns of risks related to AI agents behaving in 'unintended or unpredictable' ways
items.summary: Apple’s annual filing warns that AI agents could exceed permissions, resist instructions or take actions that are difficult to reverse.
items.body: Apple said in its annual financial filing on Tuesday that AI agents that can act in "unintended or unpredictable ways" could represent a threat to its business by opening the company up to lawsuits or hurting its reputation. The new risk factors in Apple's filing show the disruptive potential of AI agents, which have rapidly become top of mind for Silicon Valley's most important companies. "In particular, artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions," Apple wrote in the filing .

items.body: WASHINGTON/NEW YORK -- Polling has opened for the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, with control of both chambers of Congress in the balance. In the weeks leading up to election day, projections have overwhelmingly favored the opposition Democratic Party to take control of the House of Representatives from President Donald Trump's Republican Party, while the battle for the Senate is expected to be much closer. Results, particularly for the Senate, could hinge on a small number of close races, including in Alaska, where polls don't close until after midnight Eastern time. items.summary: The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.
items.body: The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly. There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost. The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.

items.title: Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
items.summary: Rio Tinto is jointly funding a A$28m "toad containment zoe" to protect the Pilbara region.
items.body: Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation. The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south. While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem. Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore. The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.

items.title: Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide
items.summary: Retailer acquires robot-assisted warehouse and intends to have UK service up and running before end of 2027 Primark is to begin making home deliveries by the end of next year as it aims to win new shoppers after a slide in profits. George Weston, the boss of the cut-price…
items.body: Primark is to begin making home deliveries by the end of next year as it aims to win new shoppers after a slide in profits. George Weston, the boss of the cut-price fashion chain’s owner Associated British Foods (ABF), said it had brought forward the launch of Primark’s home delivery plans by about two years. The company was able to speed up the process by snapping up a robot-assisted warehouse in Sheffield from Debenhams, the owner of Boohoo, PrettyLittle Thing and Karen Millen. Primark will take over the warehouse by the middle of next year and is working on preparing its suppliers to provide stock suitable for sending out to individual shoppers as well as the usual bulk orders for stores. Primark already offers a click and collect service in the UK which it has gradually rolled out since 2022 . The service is not available to its stores in mainland Europe.

items.title: China-US AI investment gap narrower than figures suggest: report
items.summary: The AI investment race between China and the US is closer than headline figures suggest, even though the technology is expected to make a greater contribution to economic growth in America, according to a Chinese think tank. The findings come as artificial intelligence becomes a…
items.body: The AI investment race between China and the US is closer than headline figures suggest, even though the technology is expected to make a greater contribution to economic growth in America, according to a Chinese think tank. The findings come as artificial intelligence becomes a focal point of technological competition between Beijing and Washington, with investment levels, computing power and the commercial applications of AI all under greater scrutiny. According to a report released recently by a research team affiliated with China Finance 40 Forum, in terms of capital expenditure by major technology firms – a common metric for gauging AI investment – China will spend about one-eighth as much as the United States this year. But the report argued that comparison gave an incomplete picture.

Those efforts have included lawsuits, an attempt to implement a new U.S. Postal Service rule for mail-in ballots this year, threatening letters to state election officials and a plan to increase the number of poll monitors. On Tuesday afternoon, The New York Times reported that the Department of Justice had sent letters to about 20 Democrats, among them prominent election lawyer Marc Elias, informing them that they might be targets in a criminal investigation of how a candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan ended up on the ballot of the Alaska Senate race.

items.title: Asda hires ex-Morrisons boss in bid to grow firm
items.summary: David Potts takes charge of Asda, which is based in Leeds, with immediate effect.
items.body: Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain. Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain. Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers.

items.title: UK and EU agree deal to remove Brexit checks on food and animal products
items.summary: Agreement to ease rules on food imports and exports is expected to come into force in first quarter of 2028 The EU and the UK have completed their deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products ranging from sausages and cheese to leather goods…
items.body: The EU and the UK have completed their deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products ranging from sausages and cheese to leather goods and flowers. A wider series of mini-deals expected to be sealed at a UK-EU summit on 20 November would also result in Britain once again contributing to the EU budget as the price of rejoining a single electricity market. It will prove a boon for British food exporters and will also mean smaller retailers in the UK such as delicatessens can return to buying smaller batches of cheese and wines, something that became impossible because of the cost of Brexit checks introduced in 2022.

items.summary: China and Oman have agreed to deepen cooperation in BeiDou satellite navigation, artificial intelligence and the digital economy, as Beijing seeks to expand the overseas applications of its home-grown technologies during the Sultan of Oman’s historic first visit to China.…
items.body: China and Oman have agreed to deepen cooperation in BeiDou satellite navigation, artificial intelligence and the digital economy, as Beijing seeks to expand the overseas applications of its home-grown technologies during the Sultan of Oman’s historic first visit to China. Analysts said the agreements reflected Beijing’s efforts to tap potential infrastructure opportunities in Oman as the Gulf state’s strategic importance grew amid the Middle East conflict. The agreements were signed during the trip to China by the Sultan of Oman, Haitham bin Tariq, during which he met President Xi Jinping in Beijing. According to their joint statement, the two countries signed 14 memorandums of understanding, covering areas including central bank digital currencies, the BeiDou satellite navigation system, space technology and supply chain investment.

items.title: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
items.summary: Wall Street weighs how the 2026 midterms could affect stocks, Treasury yields, artificial intelligence, energy prices, banks, defense and healthcare.
items.body: The stock market is not yet pricing in a Democratic sweep of Congress — despite some polls and most prediction markets pointing that way — so that scenario could weigh on share prices Wednesday, according to investors and analysts. Republicans managing to keep control could cause a short-term relief rally, they said. Short-term moves aside, the typical post-midterm pattern in the months ahead is bullish. But some wonder if the market could buck the positive historical trend this time because the S&P 500 is already up so much this year going into the election. As far as certain stocks to watch, a big Democratic win on Tuesday night — especially in the Texas governor race — could add fuel to an artificial intelligence stock sell-off on the notion that more data center restrictions would gain momentum nationally. Defense stocks could come under pressure on fears of limits on spending.

items.title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
items.summary: Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, a report has found.
items.body: The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found. Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report. The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic. "This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation. Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.

items.title: Car finance: Barclays becomes first big lender to offer payouts for mis-selling of loans
items.summary: Bank to make ‘early settlement’ offers before outcome of legal battle, with those who accept likely to get money before Christmas Barclays will this month start offering compensation to tens of thousands of people who claim they were mis-sold car loans, with some of those who…
items.body: Barclays will this month start offering compensation to tens of thousands of people who claim they were mis-sold car loans, with some of those who accept likely to see the money land in their account before Christmas. Amid an ongoing legal battle over an industry-wide compensation scheme for victims of the UK’s car finance scandal, Barclays has become the first big UK lender to break cover and begin offering payouts to some customers who have complained. Under the rules, “early settlement” offers of this kind must at least match what people would receive under the multibillion-pound scheme that is being challenged – which may help to address fears that banks might try to make “lowball” offers. But consumers face a tricky decision as, depending on the outcome of the legal battle, they could end up with more money, less money or nothing at all if they decide to decline the offer and wait.

items.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
items.summary: The men and women who rummage through commercial bins to take clothes and other items.
items.body: Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket. On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters. Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it. Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come. During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist. Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says.

items.title: UK’s most polluting power plant could power country’s largest AI datacentre
items.summary: Drax’s FTSE 250 owner strikes £20bn deal to build infrastructure in what it says is site’s ‘next chapter’ Britain’s most polluting power plant could soon power the country’s largest datacentre under a £20bn deal to build AI infrastructure on the site of the Drax power plant in…
items.body: Britain’s most polluting power plant could soon power the country’s largest datacentre under a £20bn deal to build AI infrastructure on the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire. The power plant’s FTSE 250 owner has struck a deal with the infrastructure investor Brookfield and ⁠and the AI infrastructure platform Radiant to develop a datacentre with an eventual capacity of more than 1 gigawatt that could begin operations by early 2028. In the initial phase, Drax will provide the datacentre project with land and access to the national power grid through existing connections on the site, but it hopes to begin powering the datacentre directly by the early 2030s. Drax said the development could attract more than £20bn ($26.8bn) in investment and represent “the next chapter” for the former power plant after ministers signalled plans to limit its power generation in the future.

items.title: China moves to simplify forex settlements, ease cross-border business
items.summary: China plans to expand foreign exchange settlement services and streamline cross-border trade payments, in a move to lower transaction costs and facilitate international commerce. The State Administration of Foreign Exchange (Safe) on Monday released a draft notice for public…
items.body: China plans to expand foreign exchange settlement services and streamline cross-border trade payments, in a move to lower transaction costs and facilitate international commerce. The State Administration of Foreign Exchange (Safe) on Monday released a draft notice for public consultation outlining nine measures to facilitate current-account foreign exchange transactions. The proposals aimed to “broaden the applicable scenarios, scope and types of services” and “further reduce businesses’ fund settlement and transaction costs”, according to the regulator. Among the key measures is a plan to roll out nationwide, from January 1, a scheme facilitating foreign exchange receipts and payments for cross-border trade. The programme has so far operated on a pilot basis.

items.title: AMD has been crushed into earnings. Here’s one way to trade it
items.body: Advanced Micro Devices has been under significant pressure leading up to earnings after the close. The stock has been caught in the swings of the AI debate all year, but this most recent leg lower was triggered by a wave of disappointing tech earnings. A record drop in Alphabet last Thursday was followed by weak results from Amazon, as well as AMD's long-standing CPU rival, Intel. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue well below consensus and expects the PC slowdown to last through at least the first half of next year. That sent Intel's stock down 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s. Caught in the fallout of Intel and the broader tech sector, AMD fell 10.9% that day and slid another 7.5% Monday. For the past week, AMD has traded on other companies' news. Now its own numbers get a vote.

items.body: John Lewis has turned to a celebrity best known for playing aristocrats to put a playful but rather upmarket spin on the countdown to Christmas with this year’s festive ad, which features a toy dog called Pickles and a glamorous granny. Kristin Scott Thomas, known for playing upper-crust characters in films such as Four Weddings and a Funeral and the Apple TV show Slow Horses, is cast as Gloria, a grandmother searching for gift inspiration, with the tagline “don’t give up on giving”. In the 20th version of its blockbuster Christmas ad, the department store kickstarts the official countdown to Christmas by tugging at the heartstrings, with Pickles, voiced by the comedian Paul Whitehouse, challenging Gloria to “do better than cash” when choosing a gift for her grandchildren.

items.title: Indonesia’s severe drought threatens to disrupt China’s vast battery industry
items.summary: A severe drought in Indonesia is slowing output of a crucial material used to manufacture electric vehicle (EV) batteries, creating risks across China’s vast electric car supply chain. Indonesia is a vital link in the global electric car supply chain. The Southeast Asian nation…
items.body: A severe drought in Indonesia is slowing output of a crucial material used to manufacture electric vehicle (EV) batteries, creating risks across China’s vast electric car supply chain. Indonesia is a vital link in the global electric car supply chain. The Southeast Asian nation is the world’s biggest production hub for nickel, a metal that is converted into a component used in lithium-ion batteries. But a sharp drop in rainfall in the country is causing local nickel refineries to reduce output, a move that could “add uncertainty … across the battery materials value chain”, according to market analysis firm CRU Group. The refineries require huge volumes of water to extract nickel through a process known as high-pressure acid leaching.

items.title: A little-known biotech’s high-stakes cancer bet just paid off and its shares doubled
items.summary: Genmab’s shares have doubled in three months after a string of cancer drug trial wins, strengthening its push to own more of the medicines it develops.
items.body: Danish biotech Genmab has seen its shares double in three months after a string of major cancer drug trial successes, giving fresh momentum to its push to take greater control of the medicines it develops and sells. Shares in the roughly $35 billion company surged 48% last week, including a 29% jump in a single session after strong results for petosemtamab, its experimental head and neck cancer treatment. The announcement marked Genmab's third successful Phase 3 trial in October, following positive results for treatments targeting ovarian cancer and lymphoma.

items.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
items.summary: US government agencies and cyber analysts have blamed Pyongyang for the record-breaking heist.
items.body: North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric". Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history. This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.

items.title: Guaranteed pension income ‘resurrected’ for 17m private sector workers
items.summary: Ministers propose new guided retirement scheme to help give savers protection for life Millions of private sector workers will be offered a guaranteed pension income for life under new rules designed to help them get the most out of their retirement savings. Over the past 30…
items.body: Millions of private sector workers will be offered a guaranteed pension income for life under new rules designed to help them get the most out of their retirement savings. Over the past 30 years, the majority of final salary pension schemes offering a set payout for life have closed. Workers have instead saved into a scheme and arrived at retirement with a pot of money they have to decide what to do with. George Osborne scrapped the obligation to buy an annuity – a product offering an income for life – leaving many savers wondering how to manage their money. Proposals outlined by the government on Tuesday will bring in a default option for retirees, designed to ensure that the money they have saved provides them with an income for life.

items.title: As sales slow, Chinese carmaker courts controversy with overt marketing tactics
items.summary: Chinese carmakers’ marketing tactics are under the spotlight after a controversy surrounding a comment by an Xpeng employee drew harsh criticism from middle-aged consumers. The incident comes as regulators step up quality checks on the reliability of automotive companies,…
items.body: Chinese carmakers’ marketing tactics are under the spotlight after a controversy surrounding a comment by an Xpeng employee drew harsh criticism from middle-aged consumers. The incident comes as regulators step up quality checks on the reliability of automotive companies, according to industry officials and analysts. During a live-streamed new model launch ceremony on October 15, an Xpeng product manager used the term lao deng – a slang term referring to middle-aged people who appear to be old-fashioned but arrogant – to satirise the designs of some new cars that could not attract young buyers. The comment provoked ire among some consumers in their 40s or 50s who viewed it as a derogatory statement. The product manager apologised to the public a week later, saying she meant only to criticise the rigid thinking of some conservative car designers.

items.title: JetBlue raises bag fees for third time in a year as fuel costs bite
items.summary: JetBlue raised baggage fees for the third time in a year as fuel costs continued to climb.
items.body: JetBlue Airways has raised the price of checking a bag for many customers for the third time in less than a year as high fuel costs continue to eat into the industry's profits. Checking a first bag for travelers booked in economy will now be $50, up from $45, if purchased more than 24 hours before departure during a nonpeak travel period. If it's paid within 24 hours of departure, the fee will be $60. During a peak period, such as during the holidays or the summer, it will be $55 if purchased more than 24 hours before departure, up from $49, and $70 for within 24 hours of departure. There are exceptions to the checked bag fees, such as for customers who hold a co-branded JetBlue credit card or who hold elite frequent flyer status. "We're adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in a statement.

items.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
items.summary: The tech giant reports strong sales but admits "constraints" are affecting supplies of the iPhone Duo.
items.body: Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period. The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000. The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance". Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres. Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.

items.title: Food suppliers in UK hit by cyber-attacks after freezers targeted in Europe
items.summary: Cybersecurity experts say national impact ‘minimal’ but incidents may represent the ‘foothills’ of a wider threat Food suppliers in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised the temperatures of supermarket freezers across Europe. The UK’s National Cyber Security…
items.body: Food suppliers in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised the temperatures of supermarket freezers across Europe . The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NSCS) said it was working with the affected companies but the national impact was minimal. Speaking at the launch of the NCSC’s annual review on Tuesday , its director of operations, Paul Chichester, said: “We’re aware of those incidents in the UK, and obviously we’re working with the affected organisations. We’ll keep monitoring that. At the moment, the impact is minimal.” Cybersecurity experts meanwhile reported that attacks on “dummy” fridge controls – deliberately placed online to lure would-be hackers – displayed characteristics similar to malicious operations linked to Russia.

items.title: Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail
items.summary: The annual Christmas collection of five stamps feature scenes from the Nativity.
items.body: Royal Mail has unveiled its Christmas stamps for this year - featuring scenes from the Nativity. The series of five stamps have been jointly created by graphic designer Gareth Howat and illustrator Rebecca Sutherland. The stamps depict familiar scenes of Mary and Joseph travelling, baby Jesus, an angel, the shepherds and the Three Wise Men. This year's collection marks the 60th anniversary of the first-ever Christmas special stamp. Sutherland said it was an "absolute honour" to be given the opportunity to illustrate the Christmas stamps for the Royal Mail. She said she has loved stamps since she was a child and had even collected them. "Being asked to create a set myself feels incredibly special," she added. The Christmas stamps from recent years have featured snowy scenes of UK cathedrals, or lyrics from famous carols - although 2025 also showed scenes from the Nativity.

items.title: Primark lacks fizz as it approaches its go-it-alone moment
items.summary: After a profits dip, the chain’s demerger from its sister food company still makes sense but is unlikely to reveal tons of value Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide The business logic for demerging Primark from Associated British Foods’…
items.body: T he business logic for demerging Primark from Associated British Foods’ greater Ovaltine-to-Twinings empire – an event due to happen by the end of next year – is impeccable. Read this year’s results statement and you wonder why the controlling Weston family took 20 years to get behind the idea. One paragraph can be about a yeast plant in India or the impact of high gas prices on sugar-refining margins; the next can jump to Primark’s new “digital flywheel” or the progress of the “By Coleen” collection. Even by conglomerate standards, food staples and discount fashion has always been an odd mix. Separating into two FTSE 100 companies, with stand-alone governance, makes sense. But it would be hard to say the rejig will reveal tons of value, another reason conglomerates often give for doing the splits.

items.title: The next wave of luxury real estate: marina developments with yacht parking
items.summary: Marinas are becoming the next big draw for luxury real estate, as the global wealthy search for homes to park their ever-larger yachts.
items.body: Marinas are becoming the next big draw for luxury real estate, as the global wealthy search for homes to park their ever-larger yachts, according to developers. With the number of yachts surging since Covid-19, real estate developers and investors are rushing to fill the shortage of boat slips and marina communities. There are now over 6,000 superyachts over 30 meters (98 feet) around the world, and another 200 delivered every year, according to SuperYacht Times. The growth in the size and number of yachts has created a shortage of yacht slips. And investors are rushing to fill demand. Last year, Blackstone paid $5.6 billion for Safe Harbor Marinas, which then paid $1.5 billion in August for 65 marinas and storage sites purchased from MarineMax. European private equity firms are also on a marina buying spree to fill the shortage in the Mediterranean.

items.title: Keeping mortgage interest relief approved
items.summary: Homeowners can get tax relief of £3,500 on the money spent on the interstate of a mortgage.
items.body: A move to keep tax relief on interest paid on mortgage payments has been approved. Deputy Aidan Matthews, who brought the amendment to the Budget in Guernsey, said it was currently the "worst possible time" to consider phasing out the tax relief. It also meant that the phased withdrawal of the relief, which was agreed in 2015, would also stop, it was confirmed. The relief allows homeowners to apply for tax relief on any interest paid on the mortgage of their principle residence of up to £3,500 a year. Speaking against the move, Deputy Neil Inder said that, while the idea was right in isolation, if all amendments were approved, it would add "£20m to the budget". Alderney representative Alex Snowdon said the timing of the amendment was "important".

items.title: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng says hackers used fake job interviews, AI tool to steal $6.3 billion in crypto
items.summary: Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, according to a security report the crypto exchange issued Tuesday.
items.body: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. "In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ...

items.title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
items.summary: The interest rate set by the Bank of England affects mortgage, loan and savings rates for millions.
items.body: Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting. Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings. Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe. Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people. An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it. The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.

items.title: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
items.summary: After a second apparent cyber-attack in weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned , their thermostats remotely…
items.body: Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned , their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F). The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SuperValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia. It appeared to be a reprise of attacks three weeks ago when French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software. Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases.

items.title: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue
items.summary: CrowdStrike launched an AI kill switch that the company says can stop internal agents, block relaunches and cut enterprise network access.
items.body: The cybersecurity vendor on Tuesday launched an AI kill switch designed to let security teams stop internal AI agents that go rogue, block them from relaunching and cut off their enterprise network access. The tool is built into CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian platform, launched in September to secure AI agents. CrowdStrike also announced an integration with Anthropic's Claude Cowork . "Having the ability to control and turn off, and make a decision and decide, I think that's really important for this next chapter of AI adoption," Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard told CNBC. A string of recent high-profile cyber incidents has added urgency to calls for some kind of emergency shutdown mechanism. The Hugging Face breach orchestrated by rogue OpenAI agents in July was particularly alarming for businesses.

items.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
items.summary: Millions could be entitled to compensation as a result of commission arrangements between lenders and dealers.
items.body: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.

items.title: Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices
items.summary: iPhone maker says decision to raise prices has offset some of impact, as revenues are stronger than expected Business live – latest updates Apple has warned of an “unprecedented” rise in memory chip prices, as it battles with datacentres to lay its hands on supplies. The iPhone…
items.body: Apple has warned of an “unprecedented” rise in memory chip prices, as it battles with datacentres to lay its hands on supplies. The iPhone maker’s shares fell in after-hours trading after it told investors that the higher prices will eat into its profit margins. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” John Ternus, Apple’s new chief executive, told a conference call on Monday, predicting that memory costs in the fourth quarter of this year would be even higher than in the previous three months. The tech industry has been gripped by “RAMageddon” for months , as demand for memory chips from AI datacentres has surged, driving up prices. Ternus said Apple’s decision to raise iPad and MacBook prices in June, followed by iPhone prices in September, had “provided some offset” for the company.

items.title: Disney plans several thousand layoffs, asks some managers to cut costs by up to 20%
items.summary: Disney expects to lay off several thousand employees in the latest round of job cuts for the entertainment giant.
items.body: Disney is planning to cut several thousand jobs, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. Some managers at the entertainment giant have been asked to reduce costs by up to 20%, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. It marks the latest round of layoffs since CEO Josh D'Amaro took the reins earlier this year. The update comes after separate plans in April to cut as many as 1,000 employees , predominantly in the marketing department, and in September to cut about 300 employees , many in human resources and technology divisions. Company executives warned of the possibility of more reductions in its August earnings report. "We remain highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise to create incremental capacity to invest for growth and are evaluating a variety of levers," D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston wrote in an Aug.

items.title: Asda appoints former Morrisons boss as chief executive as sales struggle
items.summary: David Potts to take over immediately as executive chair Allan Leighton steps back to non-executive strategic role Business live – latest updates Asda has appointed David Potts, the 69-year-old former boss of Morrisons, as its chief executive with immediate effect as it continues…
items.body: Asda has appointed David Potts, the 69-year-old former boss of Morrisons , as its chief executive with immediate effect as it continues to struggle to lift sales. The UK’s third largest supermarket said its 73-year-old executive chair, Allan Leighton, who has been running the business since 2024 , would now step back to a non-executive role focusing on “the long-term strategic agenda for the business”. Potts began his career on the shop floor at Tesco aged 16 and worked at the UK’s biggest supermarket for decades, eventually heading its UK business. He was then chief executive of Morrisons between 2015 and 2023, leaving after the supermarket group was taken private by the US investment house Clayton, Dubilier & Rice in 2021. Asda and Morrisons are struggling as they face heavy competition and high levels of debt .

items.title: Meta seeks to raise up to $25 billion in debt sale as AI spending jumps
items.summary: Meta is aiming to raise between $20 billion and $25 billion in a bond sale as the company ramps up spending on infrastructure and AI models and services.
items.body: Meta is seeking to raise between $20 billion and $25 billion in a bond sale on Tuesday as the company ramps up its spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure along with AI models and services. The debt sale is expected to be two-thirds in U.S. dollars and one-third in euros, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the details are private. Final pricing for the bond sale should come Tuesday afternoon, the sources said. Meta's bond sale comes days after S&P Global Ratings revised the company's outlook from AA- stable to AA- negative, citing "uncertainty" about its hefty capex spending and negative free cash flow. In its third-quarter earnings report last month, the Facebook parent revealed that its full-year capex will come in between $135 billion to $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its previous guidance.

items.title: Proposal for free bus service scrapped
items.summary: The one-year free bus service pilot was initially put forward as an amendment to next year's budget.
items.body: Proposals for a free bus service in Guernsey will no longer be considered for next year's budget, deputies who suggested the move have said. Deputies Sally Rochester and Ross Le Brun put the plan forward as an amendment to the 2027 budget , asking the Policy and Resources Committee for £1.9m to "enable the existing public transport service" to be made free of charge in a one-year pilot. They have now pulled the plans after "concern from [operator] Stagecoach" that increased passenger numbers could mean certain routes not coping with the additional demand. Rochester said she and Le Brun were committed to working with the Environment and Infrastructure Committee to explore plans for the future. Rochester also acknowledged the pilot would not be possible if buses were "at capacity".

items.title: Supermarket fridges hit with cyberattacks across Europe — here's what's happening
items.summary: European supermarkets have become the center of another cyberattack, with hackers remotely heating fridges and spoiling food.
items.body: European supermarkets have become the center of another cyberattack , with hackers remotely heating fridges and spoiling food. The attack caused temperatures in fridges and freezers to rise sharply, with at least one store reporting temperatures of up to 50°C (122°F) and other retailers discarding food. It's sparked concerns across the retail industry. Dutch supermarket group Ahold Delhaize had dozens of Delhaize stores affected in Belgium and Luxembourg. The Dutch supermarket giant told CNBC that there was an incident with refrigeration systems in dozens of its stores on Monday, which has resulted in food having to be discarded. It said the situation has since returned to normal with stores fully operational. Meanwhile, Colruyt Group said five of its Spar stores in Belgium were targeted, according to Reuters .

items.title: UK job satisfaction at record low amid rising frustration over pay and flexible working
items.summary: Resolution Foundation study finds workers are less willing to go ‘above and beyond for employers than a decade ago’ Job satisfaction among UK workers has dropped to a record low, according to a study that shows a growing frustration with employers over pay and flexible working.…
items.body: Job satisfaction among UK workers has dropped to a record low, according to a study that shows a growing frustration with employers over pay and flexible working. Analysis by the Resolution Foundation thinktank shows that a lack of flexible working, insecure jobs and a loss of independence have undermined how workers feel about their employment. Based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, the study found a sharp fall in satisfaction at work that translated into British workers being less willing to go “above and beyond for their employers than they were a decade ago”. Job satisfaction fell from 81% in 2015 to 74%, the lowest figure recorded in the British Social Attitudes survey since 1989, when the question was first asked. Fewer workers said they had an interesting job or one that offered the chance of advancement.

The military campaign against Iran has been kept quiet on purpose so as not to signal any intention of major combat escalation, the report said, quoting an unnamed official. items.title: RBA interest rates: Bullock says ‘pain now’ will prevent worse later as Reserve Bank hikes rates for fifth time
items.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia increases official cash rate to 4.85%, bringing it to highest level since 2008 RBA interest rates live updates: Reserve Bank cash rate decision Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has…
items.body: The Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has said that “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”, after lifting official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85% in a bid to combat persistent inflation. The RBA’s decision to hit mortgage holders for a fifth time in 2026 will intensify pressure on indebted households, but there were signs that the central bank will at least now wait through summer to gauge the impact of higher interest rates on the economy. The decision split the monetary policy board, as six members voted for a hike, while three were in favour of a steady cash rate. Financial markets halved the probability of another rate rise before Christmas to 12%, but continued to price in a roughly 30% chance of a sixth hike by May.

items.title: Sen. Chris Murphy still hospitalized after suffering a stroke over the weekend
items.summary: Sen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was still in the hospital as of Tuesday, his office confirmed.
items.body: Sen. Chris Murphy remained hospitalized Tuesday after suffering a stroke over the weekend, his office confirmed. "He's continuing to improve and heartened by the outpouring of well wishes," Josh Sorbe, Murphy's communications director, told CNBC in an emailed statement. "He early voted in Connecticut, and he encourages everyone to make their voices heard today by voting and sending a message in this defining election." His office did not offer additional details when asked about his status or his expected recovery. Murphy began experiencing stroke symptoms on Saturday while at his son's hockey game, his chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement Sunday. "He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said.

items.title: Thailand to raise tax on imported EVs to 35% as Chinese brands gain ground
items.body: BANGKOK -- Thailand will raise its excise tax on imported electric vehicles to 35% from the current 10%, as it seeks to promote local production in response to an influx of finished cars from China.

items.title: ‘It brings soul into this sterile world’: the Birmingham clubbers fighting to save their patch – and Britain’s nightlife
items.summary: Digbeth is the city’s most thriving party district, but railway upgrades could tear it apart. Here, clubbers explain why they are doing everything to stop that happening House beats ring out through the open air while a heaving crowd of young partygoers dance. Suddenly, they…
items.body: H ouse beats ring out through the open air while a heaving crowd of young partygoers dance. Suddenly, they begin to chant: “Richard Parker, Richard Parker!” You might think he is the next DJ on the set list, but in fact he is the mayor of the West Midlands and this block party has been assembled to send him a message: leave Digbeth alone. It’s Sunday night and I’m in Birmingham’s trendy party district. It’s filled with bars, warehouse clubs and storied music venues. The 1,800-strong crowd of mostly twentysomethings at the Parker event fits right in. But buzzy scenes like this may soon be a thing of the past. Under plans proposed by the Midlands Rail Hub Alliance – including Network Rail, which owns and manages railway infrastructure in Great Britain – seven nightclubs, including XOYO Birmingham, Mama Roux’s and Club Colette, could be demolished from 2030.

items.title: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
items.summary: Russia confirmed Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week and signaled a possible Trump-Putin-Xi summit, raising questions over Kyiv's role in negotiations.
items.body: Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin , Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table. Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters. Separately, first lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday. Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.

items.title: Trump promised a steel mill in this rural Iowa region. But is it all a midterm election ploy?
items.summary: Residents would welcome the development, but the president’s past false promises cast doubt on the proposal On a Monday afternoon in late September, Donald Trump gathered Iowa Republicans in the Oval Office to make a big announcement: the firm Mesabi Metallics would invest $15bn…
items.body: O n a Monday afternoon in late September, Donald Trump gathered Iowa Republicans in the Oval Office to make a big announcement: the firm Mesabi Metallics would invest $15bn to make the midwestern state the site of the largest steel mill in the country. One month later, and just days before the midterm election, word has spread in the small town of Wever, population 142, that the mill will be built somewhere nearby. And that’s been about it – no shovels in the dirt, workers on a job site or machinery on the dirt roads leading down towards the Mississippi River. Ask about the project in town, and the reaction isn’t enthusiasm, but skepticism. “More jobs,” Missy Pollpeter, 52, said of the project’s potential as she dined at the Green Bay Bar and Grill, Wever’s only restaurant. “If they bring it here,” her husband, Mike Pollpeter, 60, said as he finished a burger.

items.title: Options traders are betting heavily on these stocks ahead of election results
items.summary: Solar stocks see heavy call activity as voting gets underway
items.body: With prediction markets pricing in a big victory for Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections , traders are leaning into a group of stocks that investors often categorize as beneficiaries of left-wing leadership. Options trading in clean-energy stocks, particularly solar companies, surged on Tuesday, despite a five-month sell-off in the group that's left most of the companies in the industry group down on the year. Volume in the Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) surged to 40 times higher than usual Tuesday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. The fund, which typically trades fewer than 500 contracts a day the past month, traded more than 20,000 contracts by midday, and 99% of them were calls. The ETF rallied more than 400% from its pandemic low through the 2020 election before giving almost all of the gains back by April last year.

items.title: Why PC makers are turning back to China
items.body: Welcome to the Tech Latest podcast. Every Tuesday, we deliver the hottest trends and news from the tech sector. In this episode, host Chris Nuttall speaks with Taiwan tech correspondents Annie Cheng Ting-Fang and Lauly Li about why some PC makers are shifting production back to China after years of diversification. They discuss how AI-driven shortages are squeezing supplies of key components, why printed circuit boards and chip substrates have become critical bottlenecks, and what their award-winning reporting reveals about China's growing semiconductor capabilities.
